text:
Force two: oil. On the twenty-eighth of February, the US and Israel struck Iran. Days later, the Strait of Hormuz was closed.

Brent crude started at about seventy-two dollars. March was its biggest monthly jump since records began in 1988, more than sixty percent.

A ceasefire in April brought it back below one hundred. By mid-July it was under eighty. Then the attacks resumed.

On the ninth of October, Brent settled at one hundred and four dollars seventy-two. Hormuz is carrying roughly half its pre-war flow.

For Europe this hurts more than for America. Euro area energy inflation hit eighteen point eight percent in September.

Headline inflation is three point eight percent, the highest since 2023. The E C B has already raised rates twice this year, to two and a half percent.

Trump says there will be no attack on Iran before the midterms, and he has lined up Russian diesel to cool fuel prices.

The US energy agency expects Brent to average sixty-nine dollars in 2027, if production in the Gulf recovers.

Force three, and the one I'd watch most: bond yields. The ten-year Treasury started the year around four point two percent, and briefly dipped below four in February.

It passed four and a half in May, and hit five point three five on the seventh of October. The highest since April 2002.

Why it matters: Washington will pay about one trillion dollars in interest this year. The deficit is about one point nine trillion.

It also makes stocks look expensive. Based on ten-year average earnings, the S and P five hundred earns about two point four percent of its price.

A ten-year Treasury pays five point three five. That's the biggest gap in favour of bonds since the dot-com era.

Even gold noticed. It closed at a record five thousand three hundred and eighteen dollars in January. Today it's about twenty-two percent lower, because high yields make a metal that pays nothing less attractive.

Force four: the AI market. The S and P five hundred closed 2025 at six thousand eight hundred and forty-six. Last week it hit seven thousand eight hundred and forty-four. Almost fifteen percent higher.

It fell about eight percent when the war began, and was back at a record by the fifteenth of April.

Most of the gains come from a handful of AI giants. The ten largest companies are close to forty percent of the index.

Nvidia alone is valued at around five point three trillion dollars, more than every listed company in Germany combined.

Even the president's account is in on it. His filings show ninety-four trades in the Magnificent Seven in the first quarter alone, worth fifty to seventy million dollars.

So a world ETF today is, to a large extent, a bet on AI. And on the dollar.
